situation: On television, Mariam sees a strong earthquake in Japan and a volcano erupting in Italy. In Garoua, the ground feels solid and safe.

Mariam knows that Mount Cameroon, in the South-West Region, is an active volcano. She wonders what force inside the Earth shakes the ground and makes volcanoes erupt, and why this happens only in some places.
sitQA: What is the problem raised in the situation above?
The problem is that Mariam does not know what causes earthquakes and volcanoes, and why they happen only in some places.
Name the countries and the Cameroonian volcano mentioned in the situation.
Japan, Italy and Mount Cameroon are mentioned.
Why is it useful to know where earthquakes and volcanoes happen?
It helps people to build safely, to prepare for disasters and to avoid danger when they travel or settle.

qa.q: Study the map of the plates.
What is the theory of plate tectonics?
qa.a: It is the theory that the outer shell of the Earth (the crust and the top of the mantle) is broken into large, rigid plates that move slowly.

qa.q: On which plate is Cameroon? Name three other major plates.
qa.a: Cameroon is on the African Plate. Other major plates are the Eurasian, the Pacific and the South American Plates.
The plates move on the hot, partly melted upper mantle. Convection currents in the mantle and the pull of sinking plates move them a few centimetres each year.

sum.title: I. Meaning and Main Ideas
defs: Plate tectonics is the theory that the outer shell of the Earth (the lithosphere) is divided into large, rigid plates that move slowly.
items: A. The Plates
There are seven major plates and many smaller ones. Cameroon is on the African Plate.
plates_map.png
B. Movement of the Plates
– The plates move on the hot, partly melted upper mantle.
– Convection currents in the mantle help to move them.
– They move 2 to 10 cm a year, about the speed at which our fingernails grow.

qa.q: Study the three types of plate margins.
What happens at a constructive margin? Give an example.
qa.a: The plates move apart. Magma rises and forms new crust. Examples: the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and the East African Rift Valley.

qa.q: What happens at a destructive margin? Give an example.
qa.a: The plates move towards each other. One plate sinks under the other (subduction). This forms fold mountains, volcanoes and earthquakes, as in the Andes and Japan.

qa.q: What happens at a conservative margin?
qa.a: The plates slide past each other. No crust is made or destroyed, but strong earthquakes happen, as on the San Andreas Fault in California.

sum.title: II. Plates and Plate Margins
defs: A plate margin (or boundary) is the edge where two plates meet.
items: A. Constructive (Divergent) Margins
Plates move apart; magma rises and forms new crust. Landforms: ocean ridges and rift valleys (Mid-Atlantic Ridge, East African Rift).
plate_margins.png
B. Destructive (Convergent) Margins
Plates move together; one plate sinks under the other (subduction). Landforms: fold mountains, deep trenches, volcanoes and earthquakes (Andes, Japan, Himalayas).
C. Conservative (Transform) Margins
Plates slide past each other. No land is made or destroyed, but earthquakes are strong (San Andreas Fault, USA).

evaluation: A plate is a large, rigid piece of the outer shell of the Earth that moves slowly.
Subduction is the sinking of one plate under another at a destructive margin.
Why is the East African Rift Valley found at a constructive margin?
It is found there because the plates are moving apart and the land in between sinks.
remediation: The outer shell of the Earth is broken into ______.
Plates move on the hot upper ______.
At a ______ margin, plates move apart.
At a destructive margin, one plate sinks: this is ______.
The San Andreas Fault is a ______ margin.
end.remediationAnswers: 1. plates 2. African 3. mantle 4. constructive 5. subduction 6. conservative
end.homework: Ask your parents or read about Mount Cameroon: when did it last erupt, and what did the lava do?
end.homeworkTag: This prepares Lesson 11: Volcanoes and Volcanic Features.
teacherNote: Correction 1: the source notes give Mount Cameroon as an example of a destructive (subduction) margin. This is wrong. Mount Cameroon lies on the Cameroon Volcanic Line, far from plate margins, inside the African Plate. It is studied in Lessons 11 and 12.
Correction 2: plates do not "float on semi-liquid magma". They move on the hot, weak, partly molten upper mantle (asthenosphere).
The usual count is seven major plates (African, Antarctic, Eurasian, Indo-Australian, North American, Pacific, South American), not "about 12".
references: National Geography Syllabus (MINESEC), Form 4 — The Structure of the Earth: Building Processes and Impacts on Man.
